notes.subject: line
notes.text: Road lines are all white, or all yellow in national parks and snowy areas; a mix of the two is almost never seen.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: All-yellow road lines are essentially unique in the Americas to this country.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: Generation 3 is a white car with no antenna; one variant has a visible black section, found nowhere else.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: Generation 4 uses a blue car.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Square concrete poles with an indent on both sides and small pinholes at the top; like Brazilian ones but with fewer supports.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Wooden poles are also fairly common.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Cars have white plates, while commercial vehicles and taxis have orange plates.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Slots are often visible at the top of signposts.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Chevrons are yellow with black arrows.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: A white front reflector and a yellow-orange back reflector; rather rare.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Orange temporary bollards with two white stripes at the top.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Bridges often have red-painted fence posts.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Regional road names start with a letter running from A to Y from north to south.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Extremely arid desert across the northern third, often bare sand and rock without any plants.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Smooth sandy eroded mountains and valleys around Arica y Parinacota.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Brownish-red soil in Atacama region, most reliable in Generation 3.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Eucalyptus plantations with a dry climate suggest southwestern Valparaíso.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Semi-arid climate with dry hills and scattered vegetation around the capital; greener with vineyards in Maule.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Puffy-needled Monterey pines are most common in Biobío.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Narrow roads lined with trees on both sides in Biobío and Araucanía.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Monkey puzzle trees grow in far eastern Araucanía.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Rolling farmland comparable to New Zealand on Isla Grande de Chiloé, with big cabbage-like giant rhubarb plants.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Southern Aysén often shows orange and red autumn colours.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: All-yellow lines on concrete road suggest Magallanes; barren, grassy, treeless land.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Dotted paint road lines are common in Los Ríos and Aysén.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Triple yellow lines appear in some national parks like Puyehue and Alto Biobío.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Clay brick walls, often with triangles on top, mark San Pedro de Atacama.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Villa O'Higgins has street signs, fences and structures made of orange-stained wood.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Poles in Arica are white with a black number; other Atacama cities use yellow paint.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Orange lamps are most common in Calama and Chañaral.
